automatic_checks.what: Structural checks run by a script on every build (src/audit.py, report in AUDIT-v0.9.md): every card has a colour and at least one source, links point at cards that exist, share links are exact, the data hash is the same in every file, counts match, and every source URL was fetched to see that it answers.
automatic_checks.not: They do not read the science. Passing them does not mean a claim is right, only that it is labelled, sourced and linked.

science_review.what: A science review means a person with the right expertise reads each claim against its sources and decides whether it is right, up to date and fairly coloured.
science_review.how_to_help: Every card has a Suggest a fix button (e-mail). Please check claims against the listed sources and say what looks wrong.

about.certainty_rule: green = established (known science, or a defined / proved result in Maths); orange = leading idea / partial progress; red = unknown / open problem. A link takes the colour of its less-certain end.

suggest_a_fix.subject: Echo Atlas fix: <Card name> (<card id>)
suggest_a_fix.note: Every card has a Suggest a fix button that opens a prefilled e-mail (section, card, card id, version, page link). Card ids: fntu/<id>, maths/<id>, history/<id>-<n>, cell/<id>, body/<id>, element/<symbol>, <section>/link/<from>><to>.

about.what_this_file_holds: Cells, evolution and life systems: the molecules of life, DNA and the genetic code, cells, the origin and evolution of life, photosynthesis, respiration, ecosystems and bodies, with the open questions (origin of life, life beyond Earth, consciousness). The Virtual Cell and Human Body explorers sit with Biology on the site; their cards are in virtual-cell.json and human-body.json.
about.already_in_this_file: This file already holds everything for this section: the facts (summary, details), the colours (certainty), the sources (title, url, type, year, link check) and the connections between ideas, including links to cards in other sections (rel / related / section_links, each with the other section name and id). Load another section file only when you want the full card on the other end of a link.
about.how_to_use: Every item has id, title, certainty, summary, details and sources (title, url, type). Full source details (year, link check) are in sources_used. A link's reason_sources are the sources on its two cards. Fact-check against the sources; flag anything that looks wrong or out of date.

nodes.title: Elements of life (CHNOPS)

history.text: August Kekulé shows carbon makes four bonds, the key to the chemistry of life.

nodes.subtitle: six elements build most of life
summary: Most of the mass of every living thing is just six elements: carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, oxygen, phosphorus and sulfur.
Carbon can make four bonds, so it builds the chains and rings of life's molecules.
details: Carbon: Each carbon atom forms four covalent bonds, giving a huge variety of molecule shapes.
Made in stars: Hydrogen comes mostly from the Big Bang; the other five were made in stars.

nodes.title: Biological macromolecules

history.text: Hermann Staudinger proposes that giant chain molecules (macromolecules) exist.

nodes.subtitle: proteins, nucleic acids, sugars, lipids
summary: Four big families of molecules build every cell: proteins, nucleic acids, carbohydrates and lipids.
Most are long chains made by linking small units together.
details: Units: Amino acids → proteins; nucleotides → DNA and RNA; sugars → starch and cellulose.
Lipids: Fats and phospholipids are not long repeating chains, but they build membranes and store energy.

nodes.title: Cell theory

history.text: Schleiden and Schwann: all plants and animals are made of cells.

nodes.subtitle: every living thing is made of cells
summary: All living things are made of one or more cells.
The cell is the basic unit of life, and every cell comes from an earlier cell.
details: Built: Schleiden and Schwann (1838–39) and Virchow (1855), after the first microscopes of Hooke and van Leeuwenhoek.
Viruses: Viruses are not cells; whether they count as alive is debated.

sources.title: Mazzarello 1999: A unifying concept: the history of cell theory (Nat Cell Biol)

nodes.title: Prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells

history.text: Édouard Chatton names the two kinds of cell: prokaryotic and eukaryotic.

nodes.subtitle: without and with a nucleus
summary: Prokaryotes (bacteria and archaea) have no nucleus.
Eukaryotic cells (animals, plants, fungi, protists) keep their DNA in a nucleus and have organelles.
details: Size: Most prokaryotic cells are about 0.1–5 µm across; eukaryotic cells are usually about 10–100 µm.
You: Your body is built from eukaryotic cells, and carries many prokaryotes too.

nodes.title: Cell membrane

history.text: Singer and Nicolson propose the fluid mosaic model of the cell membrane.

nodes.subtitle: a fluid mosaic of lipids and proteins
summary: A thin double layer of phospholipids, studded with proteins, wraps every cell.
It lets some things through and keeps others out.
details: Model: The fluid mosaic model (Singer and Nicolson, 1972): proteins float in a fluid layer of lipids.
Thin: About 5–10 nm thick.

sources.title: Singer & Nicolson 1972: The Fluid Mosaic Model of the Structure of Cell Membranes (Science)

nodes.title: DNA double helix

history.text: Watson and Crick propose the double helix, using X-ray data from Franklin and Gosling.

nodes.subtitle: the molecule of heredity
summary: DNA is two strands wound into a double helix, joined by base pairs: A with T, G with C.
The order of the bases stores genetic information.
details: Discovered: Watson and Crick proposed the structure in 1953, using X-ray data from Rosalind Franklin and Raymond Gosling.
Size: One set of human chromosomes holds about 3 billion base pairs.

sources.title: Watson & Crick 1953: Molecular Structure of Nucleic Acids: A Structure for Deoxyribose Nucleic Acid (Nature)

nodes.title: Central dogma of molecular biology

history.text: Francis Crick states the central dogma: DNA → RNA → protein.

nodes.subtitle: DNA → RNA → protein
summary: Genetic information flows from DNA to RNA (transcription) and from RNA to protein (translation).
It does not flow back from protein to DNA or RNA.
details: Stated: Francis Crick, 1958; restated in Nature in 1970.
RNA → DNA: Retroviruses copy RNA back into DNA; this fits Crick's rule, which only forbids protein → nucleic acid.

sources.title: Crick 1970: Central Dogma of Molecular Biology (Nature)
OpenStax Biology 2e, 15.5 Ribosomes and Protein Synthesis

nodes.title: Genetic code

history.text: Nirenberg and Matthaei read the first codon: UUU means phenylalanine.

nodes.subtitle: three letters for each amino acid
summary: Each three-letter codon in RNA stands for one amino acid, or "stop".
64 codons code for 20 standard amino acids, and almost all life uses the same code.
details: Cracked: Nirenberg and Matthaei read the first codon (UUU = phenylalanine) in 1961.
Shared: The near-universal code is strong evidence that all life shares an ancestor.

sources.title: Nirenberg & Matthaei 1961: The dependence of cell-free protein synthesis in E. coli upon naturally occurring or synthetic polyribonucleotides (Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. U.S.A.)

nodes.title: Enzymes

history.text: James Sumner crystallises urease and shows an enzyme is a protein.

nodes.subtitle: catalysts that speed up life
summary: Enzymes are catalysts, mostly proteins, that speed up the chemical reactions in cells.
Each one fits its target molecule at an active site.
details: Proof: In 1926 James Sumner crystallised the enzyme urease and showed it is a protein.
RNA too: Some RNA molecules (ribozymes) are catalysts as well, including the core of the ribosome.

sources.title: Sumner 1926: The isolation and crystallization of the enzyme urease (Journal of Biological Chemistry)

nodes.title: ATP

history.text: ATP is discovered (Karl Lohmann; Fiske and Subbarow).

nodes.subtitle: the cell's energy currency
summary: Adenosine triphosphate carries energy around the cell.
Splitting off its last phosphate releases energy that powers work, from muscles to building proteins.
details: Recycled: Cells remake ATP from ADP and phosphate again and again, mostly with the enzyme ATP synthase.
Parts: Adenine, the sugar ribose and three phosphate groups.

nodes.title: Cell division

history.text: Walther Flemming describes mitosis, how chromosomes split when a cell divides.

nodes.subtitle: mitosis copies, meiosis mixes
summary: In mitosis one cell becomes two identical cells, for growth and repair.
Meiosis makes egg and sperm cells with half the chromosomes, and shuffles the genes.
details: First: Before dividing, a cell copies all of its DNA.
Bacteria: Prokaryotes divide more simply, by binary fission.

sources.title: OpenStax Biology 2e, 11.1 The Process of Meiosis

nodes.title: Origin of life

history.text: Stanley Miller makes amino acids from simple gases, but how life began is still unknown.

nodes.subtitle: how chemistry became biology
summary: How non-living chemistry first became living cells is unknown.
Experiments show life's building blocks can form naturally, but no one has made life from scratch.
details: Classic test: In 1953 Stanley Miller made amino acids from simple gases and electric sparks.
When: Life was present by about 3.5 billion years ago; how it began is still open.

sources.title: Miller 1953: A Production of Amino Acids Under Possible Primitive Earth Conditions (Science)
Des Marais et al. 2008: The NASA Astrobiology Roadmap (Astrobiology)

nodes.title: RNA world

history.text: Walter Gilbert names the RNA world: early life may have run on RNA alone.

nodes.subtitle: RNA as both gene and enzyme
summary: A leading idea: early life used RNA both to store genes and to speed up reactions, before DNA and proteins.
Ribozymes show that RNA can do both jobs.
details: Named: Walter Gilbert named the "RNA world" in 1986.
Status: Widely supported but not proven; how the first RNA formed is unknown.

sources.title: Gilbert 1986: Origin of life: The RNA world (Nature)

nodes.title: Last universal common ancestor (LUCA)

history.text: A formal statistical test strongly supports one common ancestor for all life.

nodes.subtitle: the shared ancestor of all life
summary: All living things today descend from one ancestral population, called LUCA.
Its age and features are estimates, worked out by comparing genes.
details: Evidence: A formal statistical test in 2010 strongly supported universal common ancestry.
Age: A 2024 study estimated LUCA lived about 4.2 billion years ago; other estimates differ.

sources.title: Theobald 2010: A formal test of the theory of universal common ancestry (Nature)
Moody et al. 2024: The nature of the last universal common ancestor and its impact on the early Earth system (Nat Ecol Evol)

nodes.title: Three domains of life

history.text: Carl Woese and colleagues propose three domains: bacteria, archaea and eukaryotes.

nodes.subtitle: Bacteria · Archaea · Eukarya
summary: Comparing ribosomal RNA splits life into three domains: Bacteria, Archaea and Eukarya.
Archaea look like bacteria but are a separate branch of life.
details: Proposed: Carl Woese and colleagues, 1990.
Debate: Newer genome trees suggest eukaryotes grew out of the archaea, giving two primary domains.

sources.title: Woese et al. 1990: Towards a natural system of organisms: proposal for the domains Archaea, Bacteria, and Eucarya (Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. U.S.A.)
OpenStax Biology 2e, 20.1 Organizing Life on Earth

nodes.title: Endosymbiotic theory

history.text: Lynn Margulis argues mitochondria and chloroplasts were once free-living bacteria.

nodes.subtitle: mitochondria were once bacteria
summary: Mitochondria and chloroplasts began as free-living bacteria taken inside another cell.
They still have their own DNA and divide like bacteria.
details: Champion: Lynn Margulis (then Lynn Sagan) set out the case in 1967.
Relatives: Mitochondria are related to alphaproteobacteria, chloroplasts to cyanobacteria.

sources.title: Sagan 1967: On the origin of mitosing cells (Journal of Theoretical Biology)

nodes.title: Origin of eukaryotes

history.text: A genome study places eukaryotes within the Asgard archaea.

nodes.subtitle: how complex cells began
summary: Complex cells probably arose when an archaeal host merged with a bacterium that became the mitochondrion.
The closest known archaeal relatives are the Asgard archaea.
details: When: Clear eukaryote fossils are more than 1.5 billion years old; the exact start is uncertain.
Recent: A 2023 genome study placed eukaryotes within the Asgard archaea, near the Heimdallarchaeia.

sources.title: Zaremba-Niedzwiedzka et al. 2017: Asgard archaea illuminate the origin of eukaryotic cellular complexity (Nature)

nodes.title: Mendelian inheritance

history.text: Gregor Mendel publishes his pea experiments: traits pass on in fixed ratios.

nodes.subtitle: genes come in pairs
summary: Traits are passed on by separate units (genes), one copy from each parent.
Gregor Mendel found the rules by breeding pea plants.
details: Published: Mendel, 1866; rediscovered in 1900.
Laws: Segregation: the two copies separate into different sex cells. Independent assortment: different genes are often inherited separately.

sources.title: OpenStax Biology 2e, 12.1 Mendel’s Experiments and the Laws of Probability

nodes.title: Natural selection

history.text: Darwin and Wallace present natural selection; On the Origin of Species follows.

nodes.subtitle: variation + inheritance → adaptation
summary: Individuals vary; variations that help them survive and reproduce are passed on more often.
Over many generations this adapts populations to their surroundings.
details: Published: Charles Darwin and Alfred Russel Wallace, 1858; Darwin's On the Origin of Species, 1859.
Seen today: Antibiotic resistance in bacteria evolves by natural selection.

sources.title: Darwin & Wallace 1858: On the Tendency of Species to form Varieties; and on the Perpetuation of Varieties and Species by Natural Means of Selection (Journal of the Proceedings of the Linnean Society of London. Zoology)

nodes.title: Modern synthesis

history.text: Julian Huxley's book names the modern synthesis of genetics and evolution.

nodes.subtitle: Darwin + genetics
summary: In the 1930s–40s, natural selection and Mendelian genetics were joined into one theory of evolution.
Evolution became a change in how common gene variants are in a population.
details: Forces: Mutation, natural selection, gene flow and genetic drift.
Since: Molecular biology and genomics have extended it.

nodes.title: Speciation

history.text: Ernst Mayr sets out how new species form when groups stop interbreeding.

nodes.subtitle: one species splits into two
summary: New species form when populations stop interbreeding and evolve apart.
Often a barrier, such as a mountain range or a sea, separates them first.
details: Kinds: Allopatric (split by geography) and sympatric (in the same place).
Result: Over billions of years, speciation built the tree of life.

sources.title: OpenStax Biology 2e, 18.2 Formation of New Species

nodes.title: Cambrian explosion

history.text: Charles Walcott finds the Burgess Shale, full of early animal fossils.

nodes.subtitle: animal body plans appear
summary: From about 539 million years ago, most major animal groups appear in the fossil record within a few tens of millions of years.
Eyes, shells and legs show up in early fossils such as those of the Burgess Shale.
details: Roots: Molecular clocks suggest animal groups began to split earlier, in the Ediacaran.
Why: The causes are still debated: oxygen, ecology and genetic toolkits.

sources.title: Erwin et al. 2011: The Cambrian Conundrum: Early Divergence and Later Ecological Success in the Early History of Animals (Science)

nodes.title: Mass extinctions

history.text: Raup and Sepkoski pick out the big mass extinctions in the fossil record.

nodes.subtitle: the big five die-offs
summary: Five times in the last 540 million years, a large share of species died out quickly.
The latest, 66 million years ago, ended the non-bird dinosaurs.
details: Found: Raup and Sepkoski picked out the big mass extinctions in the marine fossil record in 1982.
Now: Many scientists warn that today's loss of species could become a sixth.

sources.title: Raup & Sepkoski 1982: Mass Extinctions in the Marine Fossil Record (Science)

nodes.title: Human evolution

history.text: Raymond Dart describes the Taung child, an early human relative from Africa.

nodes.subtitle: Homo sapiens, about 300,000 years
summary: Humans are primates; our closest living relatives are chimpanzees and bonobos.
The oldest known Homo sapiens fossils, from Jebel Irhoud in Morocco, are about 300,000 years old.
details: Africa: Our species arose in Africa and later spread around the world.
Cousins: Neanderthals and Denisovans were close relatives; many people carry a little of their DNA.

sources.title: Hublin et al. 2017: New fossils from Jebel Irhoud, Morocco and the pan-African origin of Homo sapiens (Nature)

nodes.title: Life beyond Earth

history.text: The Viking landers test Mars soil for life; no life has yet been found beyond Earth.

nodes.subtitle: are we alone?
summary: No life has yet been found anywhere except Earth.
Astrobiologists search Mars, icy moons such as Europa and Enceladus, and the air of planets around other stars.
details: Why look: Liquid water, energy sources and the elements of life exist in many places.
Open: We know of only one example of life, so we cannot yet tell how common it is.

nodes.title: Photosynthesis

history.text: Jan Ingenhousz shows green plants need light to make the air fresh (oxygen).

nodes.subtitle: sunlight → sugar and oxygen
summary: Plants, algae and cyanobacteria use light energy to make sugar from carbon dioxide and water.
Oxygen is given off as a by-product.
details: Overall: 6 CO₂ + 6 H₂O + light → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6 O₂.
Old: Oxygen-producing photosynthesis evolved in cyanobacteria more than 2.4 billion years ago.

sources.title: Blankenship 2010: Early Evolution of Photosynthesis (Plant Physiology)

nodes.title: Cellular respiration

history.text: Peter Mitchell proposes how cells make ATP from a flow of protons.

nodes.subtitle: sugar + oxygen → ATP
summary: Cells break down sugar with oxygen to make ATP, giving off carbon dioxide and water.
In eukaryotes most of this ATP is made in the mitochondria.
details: How: A flow of protons across the inner membrane drives ATP synthase (Mitchell's chemiosmotic theory, 1961).
Without oxygen: Fermentation makes far less ATP from each sugar.

sources.title: Mitchell 1961: Coupling of Phosphorylation to Electron and Hydrogen Transfer by a Chemi-Osmotic type of Mechanism (Nature)
OpenStax Biology 2e, 7.1 Energy in Living Systems

nodes.title: Great Oxidation Event

history.text: Sulfur isotopes in old rocks show oxygen first built up about 2.4 billion years ago.

nodes.subtitle: life fills the air with oxygen
summary: About 2.4 billion years ago, oxygen made by cyanobacteria began to build up in the air.
It changed Earth's chemistry and paved the way for oxygen-breathing life.
details: Evidence: Changes in sulfur isotopes and in the minerals found in old rocks.
Slow rise: Oxygen stayed far below today's level for more than a billion years.

sources.title: Lyons et al. 2014: The rise of oxygen in Earth’s early ocean and atmosphere (Nature)

nodes.title: Ecosystems and food webs

history.text: Raymond Lindeman describes how energy flows between feeding levels.

nodes.subtitle: energy flows, matter cycles
summary: An ecosystem is all the living things in a place together with their surroundings.
Energy flows from producers to consumers; often only about 10% passes on to each next level.
details: Classic paper: Raymond Lindeman described energy flow between feeding levels in 1942.
Decomposers: Fungi and bacteria break down dead matter and return its nutrients.

sources.title: Lindeman 1942: The Trophic‐Dynamic Aspect of Ecology (Ecology)
OpenStax Biology 2e, 46.2 Energy Flow through Ecosystems

nodes.title: Carbon cycle

history.text: Charles Keeling starts measuring carbon dioxide in the air at Mauna Loa.

nodes.subtitle: carbon moves through life, air, sea and rock
summary: Photosynthesis pulls carbon dioxide out of the air; respiration and decay put it back.
Oceans, rocks and fossil fuels store huge amounts of carbon for long times.
details: Today: Burning fossil fuels adds carbon to the air faster than natural processes remove it.

sources.title: NASA Earth Observatory: The Carbon Cycle

nodes.title: Homeostasis

history.text: Walter Cannon names homeostasis: the body keeps its inside steady.

nodes.subtitle: keeping the inside steady
summary: Living things keep their inside conditions, such as temperature and blood sugar, within narrow limits.
Mostly by negative feedback: a change triggers a response that reverses it.
details: Named: Walter Cannon coined the word in the 1920s (reviewed in 1929).
Example: Human body temperature is held near 37 °C.

sources.title: Cannon 1929: Organization for physiological homeostasis (Physiological Reviews)

nodes.title: Nervous system

history.text: Hodgkin and Huxley explain the nerve signal (action potential) with equations.

nodes.subtitle: neurons send electrical signals
summary: Neurons carry fast electrical signals, called action potentials, along their axons.
At synapses, chemical messengers pass the signal on to the next cell.
details: Explained: Hodgkin and Huxley described the action potential with equations in 1952.
Physics: The signal is charged ions (sodium and potassium) flowing through channels in the membrane.

sources.title: Hodgkin & Huxley 1952: A quantitative description of membrane current and its application to conduction and excitation in nerve (The Journal of Physiology)

Several scientific theories compete, and experiments to test them are under way.
details: Theories: Global workspace, higher-order, integrated information and others (reviewed in 2022).
